findings.evidence: Bulging L5/S1 intervertebral disc with impingement of the traversing right S1 nerve root was underestimated on standard grayscale axial CT.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Axial grayscale CT from a 58-year-old man showing L5/S1 disc bulge and right S1 nerve root impingement, directly captioned as a manifestation of lumbar disc herniation. b: Axial colour-coded dual-energy CT electron-density reconstruction showing right S1 nerve root impingement in the same patient, supported by the caption and article focus on lumbar disc herniation. c: Axial T2-weighted MRI confirming right S1 nerve root impingement and showing L5/S1 disc herniation in a patient with lower back pain and right lower limb paraesthesia.
panels.attribution_text: Basavaraju et al. Diagnostic performance of dual-energy CT with electron-density reconstruction for lumbar disc herniation.. SA journal of radiology 2024. doi:10.4102/sajr.v28i1.3000. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: A 58-year-old man who presented with lower back pain and paraesthesia in the right lower limb: (a) Bulging L5/S1 intervertebral disc with impingement of the traversing right S1 nerve root was underestimated on standard grayscale axial CT. (b) Diagnosis of spinal nerve root impingement was made by all readers on the axial colour-coded electron-density reconstruction images. (c) Spinal nerve root impingement was confirmed on axial T2-weighted MRI (red arrow).
in_text_mentions: For the detection of spinal nerve root impingement, higher overall sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and accuracy were noticed when comparing DECT ED reconstructions with standard CT, taking clustering into account (Table 3) (Figure 3 and Figure 4). The p-values were < 0.05 for sensitivity, NPV and accuracy for all readers. Inter reader agreement was almost perfect for ED images (k = 1) and substantial for standard CT (k = 0.79).

B: Transverse T2-weighted MRI of the lumbar spine from a patient with lumbar disc herniation, showing herniation measurement annotations.

MRI Predictors for Improvement Without Any Intervention of Clinical Symptoms in Patients With Lumbar Disc Herniation, Questioning the True Need for Surgery.. panels.figure_caption: Demonstration of disc and herniation measurements on sagittal (A) and transverse (B) T2‐w images.
in_text_mentions: Sagittal T2‐w images were used to measure disc length (from anterior to posterior edge of the junction of two adjacent vertebral bodies) and to measure disc height in three regions: the anterior and posterior disc height at the junction of the anterior and posterior edges of the vertebral bodies, respectively, and the middle disc height (MDH) at the midpoint of the disc length (Figure 1(A)).

Based on the transverse T2‐w images, the length of the herniation, the greatest distance of the herniation from its base (depth), and the area of the herniation in this layer were measured (Figure 1(B)).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Sagittal CT of a pediatric patient showing a small posterior osseous fragment at L1–2 (red arrow), captioned as a ring apophysis fracture associated with pediatric lumbar disc herniation. The fracture is directly attributed to the disc-herniation disease context in the caption and in-text mentions. Upper lumbar level (L1–2) is explicitly described as exceptional in the cohort, hence atypical location. The ring apophysis fracture and osseous fragment are not represented in the allowed vocabulary, so they are proposed as findings. B: Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of the same pediatric patient showing a posteriorly extruded disc herniation at L1–2 with indentation of the ventral thecal sac, matching the configured disease lumbar disc herniation; upper lumbar location described as exceptional in the cohort (atypical).

panels.figure_caption: Ring apophysis fracture associated with pediatric lumbar disc herniation at L1–2. This case was selected because it clearly demonstrates the ring apophysis fracture; however, upper lumbar disc herniations were exceptional in our cohort. (A) A sagittal computed tomography image demonstrates a small posterior osseous fragment at the L1–2 level, indicated by the red arrow, consistent with a ring apophysis fracture. (B) A sagittal T2-weighted magnetic resonance image of the same patient demonstrates an associated posteriorly extruded disc herniation at L1–2 with indentation of the ventral thecal sac. This figure illustrates the complementary role of computed tomography in depicting the ring apophysis fracture and magnetic resonance imaging in demonstrating the associated disc herniation and neural compression.

in_text_mentions: A 65-year-old woman presented with mild left lower extremity pain for 4–5 weeks that worsened after about one week. The visual analog scale (VAS) pain score was 7. No sensory disturbances and upper motor neuron signs were documented. A lumbar spine MR scan showed that the L5–S1 intervertebral disc was slightly herniated to the rear left (Figure 1). The patient underwent a lumbar L5–S1 intervertebral disc collagenase injection 28 hours after presentation.

Analgesic medication achieved a certain degree of pain control in all patients, and no patient had intractable pain at the time of surgery. The mean duration from the onset of symptoms to surgical decompression was 10.5 days (range, 1 to 18 days). The level of disc herniation was L4/5 in one patient, and L5/S1 in three. MRI showed that all patients had massive central LDH, and one patient had lumbar spinal canal stenosis with degeneration (Figures 1A, 1B).

in_text_mentions: Lumbar spine MRI showed a mass compressing the dura that caudally migrated at the L2-L3 level on T2-weighted sagittal image (Figure 1(a)). The mass continued to the disc and was assumed to be a lumbar disc herniation. The ventral dural line was divided into two near the disc herniation such that the herniation existed between these lines. The cauda equina was compressed by the disc herniation on T2-weighted axial images (Figure 1(b)). Intradural extra-arachnoid disc herniation was diagnosed.

in_text_mentions: A longitudinal view of the psoas major muscle was subsequently obtained, allowing the identification of the L4 vertebral body, herniated disc fragment, and hypoechoic L4 spinal nerve (Figure 2). Under ultrasound guidance, vertical compression was applied laterally at the L4 vertebral level through the psoas major muscle toward the L4 spinal nerve. This maneuver reproduced the patient’s anterior thigh pain. Furthermore, during passive 5° hip extension, the superficial fibers of the psoas major muscle glided caudally.

in_text_mentions: bar spine obtained at an external clinic on 1 April 2024 revealed disc extrusion at the L5/S1 level on sagittal-view images. Axial images also showed an extrusion extending from the central to the left extraforaminal zone, resulting in compression of the left exiting L5 and transversing S1 nerve roots (Figure 1A,B). Significant compression of the exiting nerve roots was identified within the left extraforaminal zone at the L5/S1 level (Figure 1C,D). This finding was considered the primary cause of the patient’s foot drop. No additional MRI examination was performed during the treatment period.

panels.rationale: Single sagittal post-contrast MRI panel from a case report of sequestered lumbar disc herniation mimicking a spinal tumor; it shows a rim-enhancing L4/5 extradural lesion with arrows, supporting lumbar disc herniation/sequestration. The unusual tumor-like rim enhancement makes it atypical.
panels.attribution_text: Khader et al. Sequestered Lumbar Disc Herniation Mimicking a Spinal Tumor: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.116552. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Sagittal T1 post-contrast MRI Sagittal T1-weighted post-contrast image with rim-enhancing lesion at L4/5.
in_text_mentions: ral extradural lesion at the L4/L5 level, measuring approximately 29 mm craniocaudally, 13 mm transversely, and 10 mm in the anteroposterior dimension. On axial imaging, the lesion was located lateral to the thecal sac and maintained contact with both the anterior and posterior epidural spaces. The lesion appeared isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, with peripheral rim enhancement following contrast administration. Degenerative changes of the lumbar spine were also present, including loss of intervertebral disc height and facet arthropathy (Figures 1-5).

Lumbosacral MRI revealed segmental instability due to facet joint degeneration and loss of disc space, along with marked central spinal canal stenosis at the L4–5 intervertebral disc level (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: A contrast-enhanced MRI scan was therefore planned for further evaluation. However, two weeks later, the pain in the patient’s left leg became severe with worsening low back pain, and at the same time, the left ankle joint became impossible to dorsiflex, despite none of the usual triggers. This was followed by difficulty walking due to an inability to move both ankles a few hours later. He also had urinary retention. An urgent MRI scan with no gadolinium enhancement showed an enlarged lesion (Figure 2). No abnormalities were apparent on a computed tomography scan.

panels.attribution_text: Hawkins et al. Posterior Epidural Migration of a Lumbar Disc Herniation Causing Cauda Equina Syndrome: A Case Report.. Cureus 2018. doi:10.7759/cureus.2739. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: MRI of a 40-year-old male with acute onset of progressive bilateral leg weakness, back pain, and urinary retention Sagittal T2-weighted (A) and T2-weighted with fat suppression (B) images demonstrating a large T2-hyperintense mass (white arrow, A-D) in the L4-5 epidural space. Axial T2-weighted images at the level of the L4 vertebral body (C) and L4-5 disc (D) show the mass present in the left lateral and dorsal epidural spaces, displacing the thecal sac anteriorly and to the right. The mass abuts the left L4-5 ligamentum flavum (arrowhead, C-D), but does not create an obvious connection with the facet joint. It is, however, contiguous with the dorsal aspect of the disc space (skinny arrow, D). MRI: magnetic resonance imaging
in_text_mentions: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine revealed a somewhat heterogeneous, but predominately T2-weighted, hyperintense mass in the left lateral and dorsal epidural spaces (Figure 1). There was significant lumbar stenosis present at the level of L4-5 secondary to the mass, with the rightward displacement of the thecal sac. There was no clear connection to the adjacent facet joint although the dorsal mass did seem to be contiguous with the dorsal aspect of the L4-5 disc (Figure 1D).

in_text_mentions: A 61-year-old man presented to our institution complaining of intermittent left leg pain that had begun two months earlier. The patient had a history of lung cancer and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Walking caused pain from the left buttock to the outside of the left thigh, which dissipated when he rested. Muscle strength and deep tendon reflex tests were normal, and there was no bladder or bowel dysfunction. Plain x-ray images showed degeneration of the lumbar spine, and an MRI found stenosis at the L3-L4 level due to a suspected tumor (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Sagittal T2 MRI shows an L4/L5 epidural mass compressing the left L5 root; the article title and in-text identify it as a giant lumbar disc herniation. The giant/tumor-mimicking presentation is atypical. B: Sagittal T1 post-gadolinium MRI shows the same L4/L5 epidural mass with peripheral enhancement; the case is reported as giant lumbar disc herniation mimicking spinal tumor. C: Axial T1 post-gadolinium MRI shows the L4/L5 epidural mass with peripheral enhancement; the case is reported as giant lumbar disc herniation mimicking spinal tumor.

panels.figure_caption: (A) Magnetic resonance imaging of lumbar spine in T2 sagittal without contrast identifies a symmetric epidural mass lesion (arrow) measuring 4x1.9x1.7 cm (CCxAPxT) at the epidural space of L4/L5. It shows T2W hyperintense signal and slight signal difference with the original disc. No bone erosion or destruction and the mass lesion compresses the L5 root in the left. The differential diagnosis includes epidural abscess and spinal tumor. (B and C) Magnetic resonance imaging of lumbar spine in T1 sagittal and axial with gadolinium contrast identifies that the L4/L5 epidural mass lesion shows with peripheral enhancement (arrow). CCxAPxT: Craniocaudal × Anteroposterior × Transverse
in_text_mentions: MRI lumbar spine showed a T2 heterogeneous epidural mass at the L4-L5 level, measuring 4.0×1.9×1.7 cm (craniocaudal×anteroposterior×transverse) and the lesion appears as hypointense with a core of hyperintensity (Figure 1A). A contrast-enhanced MRI with gadolinium revealed peripheral enhancement of the same lesion, confirming its epidural nature (Figure 1B, C).

source_variant.context_summary: Sagittal T2, sagittal T1 and axial T1 gadolinium MRI of the lumbar spine showing a symmetric epidural mass at L4/L5 that is T2 hyperintense and shows peripheral enhancement, compressing the left L5 root.
source_variant.figure_caption: (A) Magnetic resonance imaging of lumbar spine in T2 sagittal without contrast identifies a symmetric epidural mass lesion (arrow) measuring 4x1.9x1.7 cm (CCxAPxT) at the epidural space of L4/L5. It shows T2W hyperintense signal and slight signal difference with the original disc. No bone erosion or destruction and the mass lesion compresses the L5 root in the left. The differential diagnosis includes epidural abscess and spinal tumor. (B and C) Magnetic resonance imaging of lumbar spine in T1 sagittal and axial with gadolinium contrast identifies that the L4/L5 epidural mass lesion shows with peripheral enhancement (arrow). CCxAPxT: Craniocaudal × Anteroposterior × Transverse
